newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Zulu party in turmoil after leaders quit.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Zulu party in turmoil after leaders quit.

text.p: South African Zulu leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi is casting his Inkatha Freedom Party into turmoil by driving off senior members with his hardline, autocratic leadership, political analysts say.
Buthelezi is hoping to revive his party, ready for a tough fight in the 1999 elections with the African National Congress (ANC) of his arch-rival, President Nelson Mandela.
But on the way his high-handed methods are alienating senior Inkatha members, newspapers quoted party insiders as saying.

Three leaders announced at the weekend they were quitting, including the party's top two officials after Buthelezi -- secretary-general Ziba Jiyane and chairman Frank Mdlalose, who is also stepping down as premier of KwaZulu-Natal province, the heartland of support for the Zulu-based party.
The official reasons given for their decisions were ill health and personal matters.
Further resignations are being predicted in early February.

"There is widespread dissent in Inkatha and it is in a genuine state of crisis. It is doing badly organisationally and is in total disarray," said Alexander Johnston of the University of Natal's politics department.

"The question is, does the party have the organisational capacity to regenerate itself before the elections? It depends on whether these people being discarded are indeed dead wood, which I doubt," he told Reuters.

Inkatha's rivalry with the ANC has been the most dangerous political issue in the new South Africa, where a white right-wing threat has faded away since the one man, one vote election in 1994 brought Mandela to power as the first black president.
A decade of clashes between ANC and Inkatha supporters which killed 14,000 people in KwaZulu-Natal calmed after both sides launched a peace drive and held local elections last year.
The ANC made big gains, alarming Buthelezi and prompting an inquest whose effects are now felt.

Political analysts were sceptical as to whether Buthelezi, who pushed South Africa to the brink of chaos in 1994 by boycotting general elections until a week before polling day, would turn round his party's fortunes.
University of Zululand political professor Thabo Sabela said Buthelezi was trying to rid the party of moderates who have got too close to the ANC and acted too independently of him.
The most prominent party row has been over Buthelezi's outright rejection of a peace plan being discussed by Mdlalose and ANC leaders to end political bloodshed in KwaZulu-Natal.
But Inkatha MP Velaphi Ndlovu denied the party was in crisis.
"Inkatha is very strong and combined. We are busy putting our house in order because we want to fight the 1999 elections as a strong party.
"These analysts are talking rubbish. There is no crisis".
Inkatha has little support outside KwaZulu-Natal, home to nine million Zulus, and won only 10 percent of the national vote in 1994, giving it three cabinet seats.

The party has stayed in government with Buthelezi as interior minister. The ANC's other coalition partner, the National Party of last white president F.W. de Klerk, walked out from the government last year, saying it was being ignored.

Johnston said Inkatha could keep a role in South African politics as long as the ANC desired a broadly representative government, but doubted it could spread its power base beyond KwaZulu-Natal as long as Buthelezi was its leader.
"The quite uncompromising hostility felt by many African people towards Buthelezi means that as long as he is leader it will be quite impossible," he said.
